newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia set for Western donor talks on April 25.
newsitem.headline: Zambia set for Western donor talks on April 25.

text.p: Zambia will meet Western donors on April 25 to discuss restoring aid flows which were cut last year over changes to the constitution, Zambia's Finance Minister Ronald Penza said on Thursday.
He said the meeting, to be held in London, would be attended by representatives of Western governments, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
The meeting could also pave the way for a meeting of the Consultative Group at which donors are expected to make aid pldges for 1997.

"The meeting will be hosted by the Zambian government to discuss with donors in a setting which is neutral," Penza told Reuters. "The purpose of the meeting will be to advance Zambia's economic and political agenda for the next five years."

Western donors, led by the United States, cut aid to Zambia last year in protest against constitutional changes by the Frederick Chiluba government which effectively banned some candidates from standing in the general election, including former president Kenneth Kaunda.
Seven parties boycotted the elections, which Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) won by a landslide.
The IMF and World Bank have however continued with their programmes in Zambia because the country has met the economic benchmarks on which their support is based.

In February the IMF endorsed the country's economic performance under the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF). Under an agreement last year the IMF's endorsement means the Paris Club will cut Zambia's debt by 67 percent.
The cash-strapped government is banking on the resumption of aid to meet its expenditure requirements and expects donors to fund one third of the 1997 budget which totals $1.1 billion.
Penza said Zambia would need about $200 million in balance of payment support and $275 million in project aid in 1997.
He is confident that the April 25 meeting will lead to the restoration of normal aid flows.
"I think the outcome of the meeting will be very positive," he said.
Western diplomats are however more cautious.
"I do not think this meeting will lead to the resumption of normal aid," deputy German ambassador Axel Ziedler said.
"The donors are going to listen to the presentation of the government and after the meeting bilateral donors and the government might decide on a date for a Consultative Group meeting," he added.
Sweden's first secretary to Zambia, Ingrid Wetterqvist, said her country's aid levels to Zambia depended on the governments economic and political performance.
"In Sweden's bilateral relations with Zambia levels of assistance are still pegged to the development of the economic reform programme and progress in the area of good governance," Wetterqvist said.
"It is envisaged that further consultations on this will take place with the Zambian government in the very near future," she added.

Earlier this week the Zambian government came under diplomatic pressure once again over proposed legislation to control the media. The passing of the Media Council Bill was postponed until further consultation.
